name: Badawi al-Jabal
bio: Muhammad Sulayman al-Ahmad was born in Dayfa, a village in the al-Haffa district of Latakia province in Syria, in 1323 AH (1905 CE) according to Tatimmat al-A'lam and al-Mawsu'a al-Arabiyya, though the magazine al-Irfan described him in December 1923 as a youth of nineteen; his father, Shaykh Sulayman al-Ahmad, was a scholar of Arabic and of law. He sent his early poems to the Damascus newspaper Alif Ba', whose owner Yusuf al-Isa signed them “Badawi al-Jabal”, “the Bedouin of the Mountain”, so that people would read “the poetry for the poetry”; the name took the place of his own. He opposed the French Mandate and was imprisoned more than once, was elected to the Syrian parliament in 1937 and several times after, took refuge in Iraq in 1939, and served as minister of health in 1954 and later as minister of propaganda and information. In 1956 he left Syria and moved between Beirut, Istanbul, Vienna and Geneva, writing “The Stranger Nightingale” in Vienna, and returned in the early 1960s. In 1968 he was kidnapped and beaten almost to death; he spent the last year of his life unable to move, in the military hospital in Damascus, and died in 1401 AH (1981 CE).
